analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurers to cover at least 48 hours of hospital stay after a mastectomy.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: after being introduced and referred to the Senate health committee in March 1999, it stayed there until the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required health plans and insurers to cover a hospital stay of at least 48 hours after a mastectomy and at least 24 hours after lymph node surgery for breast cancer. It would also have stopped insurers from requiring advance permission for the stay, from paying women rebates to leave the hospital early, and from rewarding or penalizing doctors based on how quickly patients are discharged. It never received a committee hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Women undergoing breast cancer surgery and their families. A mastectomy is major surgery, and insurers in the 1990s commonly limited hospital stays to a day or less; this bill would guarantee at least two covered days, with the decision to go home early left to the woman and her doctor rather than to an insurer. Hospitals and surgeons would also gain financially from longer covered stays.

how_it_helps.text: It would prohibit group health plans and insurers from restricting hospital benefits to less than 48 hours after a mastectomy or 24 hours after a lymph node dissection, unless the woman, in consultation with her attending provider, chooses to leave earlier.

It would ban 'drive-through' practices: plans could not require insurers' pre-authorization for the stay, could not deny or drop a woman's coverage just to avoid the requirement, could not offer cash rebates to induce women to leave early, and could not penalize or reward doctors for discharging patients against the minimum.
The same protections would apply to individual (non-group) insurance, not just employer plans.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers, who would bear the added cost of covering longer hospital stays; the costs would tend to show up in premiums. The bill lets insurers keep deductibles and coinsurance, so patients could still pay some of the stay's cost themselves.

drawbacks.text: Requiring a minimum covered stay raises costs for employers and insurers, and those costs can be passed to workers through higher premiums or reduced benefits — an honest supporter would acknowledge the mandate has a price.

Critics of benefit mandates argue that one-size-federal-minimums reduce plan flexibility and that shorter stays, when chosen jointly by a woman and her doctor, can be safe; the bill already allows discharge before 48 hours by mutual decision, but the federal floor limits how far insurers can steer toward outpatient surgery.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — a guaranteed two-day hospital stay after major breast cancer surgery, unless a woman and her doctor choose otherwise — was significant for the roughly one in eight women affected by breast cancer, and it closed loopholes (rebates, provider incentives, reclassification) that would have undermined it. The cost — somewhat higher insurance premiums and a federal mandate on employers and insurers — was real but modest, and the bill preserved clinical flexibility for early discharge. A fair criticism is that a benefit mandate shifts costs into premiums rather than lowering them, which weighs hardest on the uninsured and the self-employed. On balance, the bill served patients more than it harmed anyone but insurers' cost controls.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate's health committee never acted on it, so it sat without a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Daschle introduced the bill on March 23, 1999, with ten other Democratic senators as cosponsors at introduction.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions — the only action besides its introduction.
The bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote; the record shows no further action through the end of the 106th Congress on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and self-insured employers kept full discretion over how long a woman stays in the hospital after breast cancer surgery, without a federal minimum.

for.name: Sen. Tom Daschle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks.

for.name: 11 Democratic cosponsors
for.role: Senate cosponsors (including Inouye, Lautenberg, Cleland, Johnson, Mikulski, Sarbanes, Murray, Hollings)

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican senator signed on, and the bill went no further than the Senate HELP Committee.

industries.note: The bill would bar insurers from limiting hospital stays after breast cancer surgery and from pressuring doctors with incentives or penalties to shorten them, removing a cost-control lever. It would apply in both the group and individual markets.
ERISA plans would have to cover the minimum stay and could no longer pay rebates to steer women into shorter ones, adding benefit costs to employers.

A guaranteed minimum inpatient stay after mastectomy and lymph node dissection would raise reimbursement for hospital stays following breast cancer surgery, though the bill leaves the reimbursement level itself negotiable.
